newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Freed Nigerian hostages relive detention nightmare.
newsitem.headline: Freed Nigerian hostages relive detention nightmare.

text.p: Shell oil workers held hostage by Nigerian villagers making political demands said on Thursday they were beaten by their captors and threatened with death.

The political grievances of the villagers against the military government have caught the country's oil giant Royal Dutch/Shell in the middle and threatened a possible disruption in vital oil exports.

Ijaw tribesmen seized Shell's oil flow stations on Saturday in the midwestern Delta state and held 127 Nigerian staff hostages in protest against the government's relocation of their local government headquarters from Ijaw area.

"A group of 40 Ijaws armed with automatic rifles, cudgels and crude implements attacked the Egwa flow station in flying boats and disarmed the lone policeman," said a station attendant who was among the nearly 80 hostages who have been freed.
"They flogged me with cutlasses, threatening to kill me... I'll never go back there...," said another. Both declined to be identified for fear of reprisals from the community.
Many of the hostages had been freed by Wednesday night after delicate negotiations with the communities but about 50 were still due to be released by Thursday evening.
Shell officials in Warri, headquarters of its operations in the Western region, said a flotilla of eight boats were departing soon to pick up the rest of the hostages at Egwa.
"The whole thing was a nightmare, a terrible experience," said another freed Shell staff identified only as Mesh.
The cause of the problem is a rivalry in the Warri area between three tribes -- the Ijaws, the Itsekiris and Urhobohs.
The Urhobohs controlled the affairs in the oil town in the 1970s until the following decade when the Itsekiris, who provide the ruler for Warri began to press for more say in the town.
The Ijaws, who inhabit the riverine areas and have a bigger population also began asking for more amenities in their areas.

"There is a deep-rooted rivalry among the three tribes," said John Nana, a lawyer of Urhoboh-Itsekiri parentage. "People feel that if a local government is sited in their town then they get more government patronage by way of amenities."
The Ijaw tribesmen launched the attack on Saturday demanding the headquarters of the local government should be moved back to Ogbe-Ijoh, an Ijaw town from Ogedigben, an Itsekiri town.
The situation escalated on Tuesday into riots and random shootings in Warri in which three Ijaws were killed.
Police were still patrolling the tense town on Thursday.
Simultaneously in the eastern flank of Nigeria where Shell also produces oil, the community in Nembe also shut Shell's flow station there and asked its staff to leave the facility.
The closures have cut Shell's production by 210,000 barrels per day, about 10 percent of Nigeria's overall output,

"People in the Delta area believe government does not exist in physical context," commented Steve Menta, a community leader. "It is only Shell that we see and people feel government will listen if Shell is involved."
Shell officials who negotiated the release of the hostages with the community said the attack had been carefully planned.
"Within 10 minutes of after they seized Egwa flow stations the villagers had rapidly covered the other areas," said one official.
"When we finally made contact with those in charge of the rebellion they sounded reasonable but made clear their boys were patrolling the creeks and we should not try anything funny."
